newsitem.title: SPAIN: Rato predicts electricity prices in Spain to fall.
newsitem.headline: Rato predicts electricity prices in Spain to fall.

text.p: Electricity prices in Spain will fall as a result of increased competition when the new conservative government frees up the market, Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said in an interview published on Sunday.

The government which took over in May after 13 years of Socialist rule is working on a liberalisation of the long protected electrical sector, the backbone of Spain's stock market, which will end the generous rate increases that ensured comfortable margins.

As a first move, it has announced that 66 percent state-owned Endesa will purchase up to 75 percent in regional electrical distributors in Andalucia and Catalonia in order to secure its position before full privatisation by 1999.

"The Endesa project must be seen as part of the liberalisation of Spain's electrical map, which the (ruling Popular Party) PP intends to change by introducing competition, allowing consumers to choose their power suppliers and ending the privileges of the former integrated system," Rato told the daily ABC in an interview.
Asked whether this meant consumers would pay less, he said, "Yes, as a result of greater competition."

Rato's colleague at the industry and energy ministry, Josep Pique, has already announced rate cuts from January 1 of one percent for home users and five to six percent for small- and medium-sized businesses. He said any rises thereafter would be below inflation.

If a series of deals now on the table go ahead, analysts expect giants Endesa and Iberdrola to take up 80 percent of the market, with some 15 percent for a group forming around Union Fenosa and the rest for Cantabrico group.

Rato rejected critics' charges that making Endesa take big stakes in the regional companies of Andalucia and Catalonia conflicted with the PP's stated aims to keep the state from competing with the private sector.
"Endesa, the privatised Endesa of the future, must be able to compete," he told ABC.
